paras: The McGaheysville dance dynamiting was an attack on the night of December 26, 1888, in which a dynamite cartridge exploded under a house near McGaheysville, Rockingham County, Virginia, where a party of Black people were holding a dance. The blast nearly destroyed the building and left Amos Moore and two women reported fatally injured. A Harrisonburg dispatch carried in papers across the country reported that threats of lynching followed.

According to the Harrisonburg dispatch of December 28, the cartridge was placed under the corner of the house, which some versions call the Carter House, on Wednesday night while the dance was under way. A man who saw the cartridge, with its fuse burning by the German-language account, recognized the danger and raised the alarm. All but three of the people inside escaped before the explosion. Moore and the two women, who "had not time to escape," were thrown through the building, and the dispatch said "They cannot recover."

None of the reports named the person who placed the cartridge or gave a motive. The Baltimore Deutsche Correspondent's version attributed the act to unknown villains but added that the perpetrator was believed to be known and that steps toward his arrest were under way.

The English dispatch closed with the line "Threats of lynching are freely indulged in," without saying against whom. The German version was more specific, reporting that the population was so agitated that a lynch court against the perpetrator was not improbable. No later report of an arrest, of the victims' deaths, or of any lynching appears in the coverage.

The first notice was a one-sentence item in the Wilmington Daily Republican's news summary on December 28, which placed the house in "the eastern part of Rockingham County" and said "several" inmates were reported fatally injured. The fuller Harrisonburg dispatch ran the next day, nearly word for word, in papers from Seattle and St. Paul to Omaha, Wichita, Indianapolis, Sacramento, Salt Lake City and Los Angeles. Headlines varied: the Indianapolis Journal called it "Attacking Negroes with Dynamite," the Sacramento Record-Union "The Virginia Outrage," and the Los Angeles Herald "Dynamite Becoming too Popular."

Some papers went beyond the dispatch's text: the Wichita Eagle headed it "Killed by Dynamite" although the story reported only fatal injuries, and the Great Falls Leader said the house was "blown to atoms." The Salt Lake Herald misprinted the dateline as Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, and the place as "McGlaysville." By December 31 the story had shrunk to a single line in the Maysville Evening Bulletin's news paragraphs.

accounts.label: Wire brief
accounts.gist: A house in eastern Rockingham County where colored people were having a party was blown up Wednesday night; several inmates were reported fatally injured.

accounts.label: Harrisonburg dispatch (English)
accounts.gist: A cartridge under the corner of a house near McGaheysville exploded during a dance; an alarm let all but three escape; Amos Moore and two women were fatally injured, and threats of lynching were freely made.

accounts.label: Harrisonburg dispatch (German, Baltimore)
accounts.gist: Same facts, adding that unknown villains placed the cartridge, that the perpetrator was believed known and steps to arrest him were under way, and that a lynch court was not improbable.

framing.detail: Papers ran the Harrisonburg dispatch nearly verbatim under heads such as 'Blown Up by Dynamite', 'Blew Up the House' and 'Attacking Negroes with Dynamite'.
The Sacramento Record-Union headed the item 'The Virginia Outrage' and the German Correspondent called it a 'teuflischen That' (devilish deed).
Some papers headlined it as a dynamite story ('Dynamite Becoming too Popular', 'Killed by Dynamite') without reference to race.

versions.value: Three: Amos Moore and two women

conflicts.note: The earlier brief is vaguer; the fuller dispatch names three.
The Wichita headline goes beyond its own text, which reports only fatal injuries.
The Salt Lake Herald's dateline and spelling are printing errors; its text is otherwise the same Rockingham County dispatch.
